## 1. What you'll build, and why

A function call has a cost — set up arguments, jump, return — and, worse, it's a **wall**: the
optimizer can't see that `sq(5)` is `25`, because `sq`'s body is somewhere else. **Inlining** tears
down the wall by copying the callee's body into the caller. Now `sq(5)` becomes `5*5` right there, and
the constant folder you already wrote finishes the job. Inlining is valuable less for removing the call
overhead than for **everything it unblocks** — it's the pass that turns a tower of tiny helper
functions into one flat, optimizable blob.

- **You implement:** the inline transform — splice the callee's body at the call site.
- **Outcome:** small calls disappear, the passes cascade across the boundary, and `-O` matches
  `swiftc`.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Inlining is a copy-and-rename

To inline `%r = apply @f(a₀, a₁)`, you replace it with a copy of `f`'s body, with two substitutions:
`f`'s **parameters** become the actual **arguments**, and `f`'s **return value** becomes `%r`. The only
real work is **renumbering** — `f`'s SSA values (`%0`, `%1`, …) would collide with the caller's, so you
shift them by an offset; `f`'s parameter values map to the caller's argument values instead. Then you
splice the renumbered instructions where the call was, and rewrite every use of `%r` to the callee's
returned value:

![Inlining replaces a call with the callee's body. `sq(5)` becomes `5 * 5` spliced into `main`; then constant folding — which couldn't see across the call before — collapses it to `25`, and the now-uncalled `sq` is removed.](figs/inline.png)

That's the whole transform: a value map (`param → arg`, else `+offset`), a splice, and a
result-substitution. Because we're on SSA, there's no aliasing to worry about and exactly one
definition to rewire — Phase 4's recurring gift.

### Inter-procedural: the first pass that needs the whole program

Every pass so far was **intra-procedural** — it transformed one function in isolation. Inlining is
different: it needs the *callee*, which lives in another function. So it runs as a **module-level**
transform (over `Sil.modul`), before the per-function pipeline. After inlining, callees that are no
longer called anywhere are **dead** and removed — `sq` vanishes once its only call is inlined.

### Why v0 only inlines single-block leaves

Two real hazards make "inline everything" wrong:

- **Recursion.** Inline a call to `fib` inside `fib` and you get another call to inline, forever. We
  sidestep it by only inlining **leaf** functions (no `apply` inside) — a leaf can't be recursive.
- **Block surgery.** A callee with internal control flow (an `if`) has *several* blocks and *several*
  `return`s. Splicing those means **splitting** the caller's block at the call and threading every
  `return` to a continuation block (with a block argument for the result) — doable, but fiddly. A
  **single-block** leaf has one block and one `return`, so you just splice its instructions, no
  surgery. That's the simplest safe inlining, and it already covers a huge fraction of real helpers
  (`sq`, `add`, `area`, accessors). Multi-block inlining is the v1 upgrade.

A real compiler doesn't inline *every* eligible call either — it uses a **cost model**: inline if the
callee is small, or called once, or the call is hot, but not if it would bloat the code. We always
inline our eligible callees (they're tiny); the cost model is an exercise.

### The payoff is the cascade

Run `--sil-opt` on `func sq(x){ x*x }; print(sq(5)+sq(6))`: after inlining, the two calls become
`5*5` and `6*6`; constant folding makes them `25` and `36`; folding again makes the sum `61`; DCE
sweeps the leftovers; and `sq` is gone. **One inline created work for three other passes.** This is why
inlining runs early and the pipeline runs the cleanup passes after it — and why production pipelines
sometimes inline, optimize, and inline again. The optimizer is a system; inlining is the pass that
feeds it the most.

> Oracle: swiftc's `PerformanceInliner` (with a real cost model and a "what does inlining *enable*"
> bonus) runs in the SIL optimizer; LLVM's inliner does the same on LLVM IR. Both run **before** the
> scalar passes for exactly the cascade reason.

## 3. Build it, step by step

In `opt.ml`, fill the `TODO(19)` in `inline_module`'s `inline_in` (the call-finding worklist, the
`inlinable` check, and dead-callee removal are given):

For the found call `(b, rv, args, f)`: pick `off = max_val g + 1`; let `fb` be `f`'s single block.
Build `vmap` (a parameter → its `args` entry; else `v + off`). Map `fb`'s instructions
(`List.rev fb.Sil.instrs`) through `(vmap v, map_instr vmap i)`, copying each type into
`g.Sil.val_ty`; compute `retval` from `fb`'s `Return`. Splice the inlined instructions in place of the
`(rv, apply …)` entry. Substitute `rv → retval` everywhere via `map_instr`/`map_term`. Set
`progress := true`.

Reference: `solution/opt.ml`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase4-optimizer/19-inlining
```

cram checks `sq(5)` is inlined and folded to `25` with `@sq` removed, and that `-O` (nested calls,
inlining in a loop, recursion left alone) matches `swiftc`. alcotest checks a single-block leaf is
inlined and removed, a recursive function is kept, a multi-block leaf is kept, and the result still
verifies after the full pipeline.

## 5. Benchmark it

A program built from many tiny helpers (`sq`, `add`, accessors) collapses under `-O` to flat,
constant-folded code with no calls — diff the instruction/call counts with vs without inlining. Time a
hot loop that calls a leaf each iteration: inlining removes the per-iteration call and lets the loop
body fold/CSE as a whole.

## 6. Exercises

1. **A cost model.** Only inline if the callee is "small" (instruction count below a threshold) or
   called exactly once. Add the count and the policy — and a flag to log inlining decisions.
2. **Multi-block inlining.** Handle callees with control flow: split the caller's block at the call,
   copy *all* the callee's blocks (renumbering block ids too), turn each `return v` into a branch to a
   continuation block that takes the result as a **block argument**, and continue there.
3. **Recursion via a bound.** Allow inlining a recursive call to a fixed depth (inline once, leaving
   the inner call) — useful for small base cases. Guard against blow-up.
4. **Inline + re-optimize loop.** Run inline → the scalar pipeline → inline again to a fixed point, so
   a chain `a()→b()→c()` flattens fully and each round re-exposes the next.

## 7. Recap & what's next

You built **inlining**: copy the callee's body in, renumber and bind, splice, rewire the result —
the first inter-procedural pass, and the one that feeds all the others. Small functions are free, and
`sq(5)` folds to `25` because the wall is gone.

Next, **20-llvm-opt**: hand the optimized SIL to **LLVM's** optimizer (compile at `-O2`) and measure
the generated-code runtime against `swiftc -O`. Our SIL passes did the Swift-level work; LLVM's
backend does the machine-level work (instruction selection, register allocation, scheduling). Together
they are **Milestone M4** — `swiftml -O` competitive with `swiftc -O`.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
| Some (b, rv, args, f) ->
    progress := true;
    let off = max_val g + 1 in
    let fb = match f.Sil.blocks with [ b ] -> b | _ -> assert false in
    let param_arg = List.map2 (fun (p, _) a -> (p, a)) f.Sil.params args in
    let vmap v = match List.assoc_opt v param_arg with Some a -> a | None -> v + off in
    let inlined = List.map
      (fun (v, i) -> Hashtbl.replace g.Sil.val_ty (vmap v) (Hashtbl.find f.Sil.val_ty v); (vmap v, map_instr vmap i))
      (List.rev fb.Sil.instrs) in
    let retval = match fb.Sil.term with
      | Sil.Return (Some v) -> Some (vmap v) | Sil.Return None -> None | _ -> assert false in
    let rec splice = function
      | (v, _) :: rest when v = rv -> inlined @ rest
      | x :: rest -> x :: splice rest | [] -> [] in
    b.Sil.instrs <- List.rev (splice (List.rev b.Sil.instrs));
    (match retval with
     | Some rv' -> let sub x = if x = rv then rv' else x in
         List.iter (fun (bb : Sil.block) ->
           bb.Sil.instrs <- List.map (fun (v, i) -> (v, map_instr sub i)) bb.Sil.instrs;
           bb.Sil.term <- map_term sub bb.Sil.term) g.Sil.blocks
     | None -> ())
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — cost model

`size f = Σ |block.instrs|`. Inline a call only if `size callee <= threshold` (say 10) **or** the
callee has a single call site in the whole module (computed from the apply counts). Add a `bonus` if
the arguments are constants (inlining will fold a lot) — that's swiftc's "inlining benefit" heuristic
in miniature.

### 2 — multi-block inlining

Split the caller block `B` at the call into `B` (instrs before) and a fresh continuation `C` (instrs
after + `B`'s old terminator); give `C` a block argument for the result. Copy all of `f`'s blocks with
both value and **block-id** offsets; point `B` at `f`'s entry; turn each `return v` into
`br C(vmap v)` and each `return` (void) into `br C`. Replace `rv` with `C`'s argument. mem2reg/GVN then
clean up exactly as for the single-block case.

### 3 — bounded recursion

Track an inline depth per callee; allow inlining a self-call up to depth *k*, leaving the innermost
call intact (so it terminates). Useful to specialize a couple of base-case iterations; guard total
code growth with the cost model from Exercise 1.

### 4 — inline + re-optimize

Wrap `inline_module` and the per-function pipeline in a loop with change detection: inline, run the
scalar passes, and if inlining changed anything, repeat. A chain `a()→b()→c()` flattens one level per
round; the scalar passes in between keep the IR small so later inlining decisions stay cheap.
```
